blocks.html: Fitting a model is the first step. Diagnostics then check, from the model’s own residuals and fitted values, whether the assumptions of §12.3 held in this dataset (§12.5.1) and whether one or two observations are driving the result (§12.5.2). Some problems, such as mild curvature, show far more clearly in a residual plot than in the raw scatter diagram.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Residual analysis examines the residuals (observed − fitted) with plots to check linearity, normality and equal variance. It often uses standardised residuals, each residual divided by its own estimated SD, s√(1 − h), where h is the leverage of §12.5.2. About 95% of standardised residuals should lie between −2 and +2 if the model holds.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The assumptions of §12.3 are assumptions about ε, and residuals are its observable stand-ins. If the model is right, residuals should look like random noise: centred on zero at every fitted value, with constant spread, and roughly Normal.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: For the clinic regression, residuals plotted against fitted values scatter randomly around zero with constant spread (left panel below). The right panel shows what a problem looks like: a straight line fitted to simulated data in which weight gain slows with age. The residuals form an arch, positive in the middle and negative at both ends, because the line misses the curve systematically.

blocks.alt: A healthy residual pattern and a curved problem pattern
blocks.caption: Figure 12.6. Residuals against fitted values. Left: the clinic regression of weight on age, a healthy random scatter. Right: simulated data in which weight gain slows with age, fitted with a straight line; the arch shows non-linearity.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cl  <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
fit <- lm(weight_kg ~ age_months, data = cl)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(fit)          # the four standard plots
range(rstandard(fit))                    # standardised residuals
max(hatvalues(fit)); max(cooks.distance(fit))
[1] -2.079537  2.438442
[1] 0.03463716
[1] 0.09016558

plot(fit) draws the four panels shown in §12.3: by default R gives residuals vs fitted, Normal Q-Q, Scale-Location and residuals vs leverage (R Core Team, plot.lm). The standardised residuals run from −2.08 to +2.44, as expected for 100 children. The largest leverage (0.035) and Cook’s distance (0.09) are read in §12.5.2.

points.html: Residuals vs fitted: random scatter supports linearity and equal variance; a curve means non-linearity (§12.4.5); a funnel means heteroscedasticity.
Normal Q-Q plot of residuals checks normality. The assumption concerns the residuals, not the raw outcome.
Scale-Location plot: a rising trend in √|standardised residual| is the clearest sign of unequal variance.
Look at the plots. A pattern in a plot says more than any single test statistic.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Leverage (h) measures how far a point’s predictor values lie from the centre of the predictors. In simple regression, h = 1/n + (x − x̄)²/Sxx; the leverages average (k + 1)/n. An influential point is one whose removal would substantially change the fitted coefficients. Cook’s distance measures this: D = (r_std²/(k + 1)) × h/(1 − h), where r_std is the standardised residual.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A point with an extreme x has high leverage: like a long lever, it can move the line. Whether it does depends on its residual. If its y is where the line predicts, it changes nothing. A point with both high leverage and a large residual pulls the line towards itself. Cook’s distance multiplies the two together.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Add one hypothetical, severely malnourished child weighing 8.0 kg to the 100 clinic children (figs/ch12_influence.py). If the child is 36 months old, the oldest age in the register, h = 0.031, the standardised residual is −5.7, Cook’s D = 0.52, and the slope falls from 0.150 to 0.139 kg per month. The same child at 24 months, near the mean age, has h = 0.010 and D = 0.10, and the slope stays at 0.150. Same weight, same kind of outlier; only the leverage differs.

blocks.alt: One very light child tilts the line only when it sits at the edge of the age range
blocks.caption: Figure 12.7. A hypothetical 8.0 kg child added to the 100 clinic children. Left: at 36 months (leverage 0.031, Cook’s D 0.52) it tilts the line from a slope of 0.150 to 0.139 kg per month. Right: at 24 months (leverage 0.010, D 0.10) the slope is unchanged.

blocks.html:
Worked Calculation (leverage of a 36-month-old in the original 100 children)

  1. h = 1/100 + (36 − 24.35)²/6190.8 = 0.010 + 135.7/6190.8 = 0.010 + 0.022 = 0.032.
  2. The average leverage is (k + 1)/n = 2/100 = 0.02, so this child has 1.6 times the average. The 12-month-olds are furthest from the mean age and have the largest leverage in the register: h = 0.010 + (12 − 24.35)²/6190.8 = 0.035. The largest Cook’s distance among the real children, which software lists, is 0.09, against 0.52 for the hypothetical child: no real child pulls the line noticeably.

points.html: Leverage depends only on the predictor values, not the outcome. A high-leverage point can fit the line perfectly.

Influence needs both leverage and a large residual; Cook’s distance combines them. Compare each point’s D with the rest. Refit without the point and see whether the conclusion changes: that is the direct test.

An influential point is a prompt to investigate, not to delete. If it is a data-entry error or a child who does not belong to the study population, correct or exclude it and say so. If it is a genuine child, keep it and report how much the result depends on it.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 12.6

questions.prompt: One unusual point has an extreme predictor value but lies on the regression line; another has an ordinary predictor value but a very unexpected outcome. Which has high leverage, and which a large residual? Which is more likely to be influential?
questions.answer: The point with the extreme predictor value has high leverage (leverage depends only on x). The point with the ordinary x but unexpected outcome has a large residual. Neither is strongly influential on its own: the high-leverage point lies on the line, so removing it hardly changes the fit, and the large-residual point has little leverage to tilt the line (it mainly shifts the intercept slightly). Influence needs both at once, which Cook’s distance measures.

questions.prompt: Why is an influential point a prompt to investigate rather than a reason to delete?
questions.answer: It may be a genuine observation showing real variation: deleting it discards information and makes the result look more certain than it is. Or it may be a data-entry error or a person outside the study population, who should be corrected or excluded. Only checking the record can tell which. Either way, report the fit with and without the point so readers can see how much the conclusion depends on it.

questions.prompt: In a regression of 50 adults’ systolic BP on age, x̄ = 45 years and Sxx = 8,000 years². Compute the leverage of a 25-year-old and of a 75-year-old, and compare each with the average leverage.
questions.answer: h = 1/n + (x − x̄)²/Sxx. 25-year-old: 1/50 + (−20)²/8000 = 0.020 + 400/8000 = 0.020 + 0.050 = 0.070. 75-year-old: 0.020 + 30²/8000 = 0.020 + 900/8000 = 0.020 + 0.1125 = 0.1325. The average leverage is (k + 1)/n = 2/50 = 0.04, so the 25-year-old has 1.75 times and the 75-year-old 3.3 times the average. The 75-year-old could move the line most if their BP is far from its prediction.
